news_drafts.headline: Havering pension fund underperformed benchmark by 3.41 percentage points over five years as pooling rules force London CIV rebalancing plan
news_drafts.lead: The Havering pension fund returned 4.69 per cent annually over five years against a benchmark of 8.10 per cent, the Pensions Committee heard. The fund delivered positive returns in the quarter to June, posting 6.09 per cent, but underperformed its benchmark in each reporting period. New mandatory pooling regulations that came into force on 30 June required Havering to sign an Investment Management Agreement with London CIV, the FCA-regulated asset pool managing the fund. The fund's asset allocation has drifted: listed equities stand at 45.9 per cent, at the upper limit of their 35–45 per cent tolerance range, while alternatives remain underweight — private credit at 6.3 per cent against a 10 per cent target, property at 7.0 per cent against 12.5 per cent, and infrastructure at 10.0 per cent against 12.5 per cent. Under the Investment Management Agreement, London CIV must produce a Strategic Implementation Plan within 90 days, setting out how it will rebalance the portfolio and implement the fund's investment strategy.

news_drafts.headline: Havering faces £110m schools funding deficit as high needs demand outpaces government grant
news_drafts.lead: Havering Council's high needs block, which funds support for children with special educational needs and disabilities, is overspending by £45m in the current year and faces a cumulative deficit forecast to reach £110m by 2027/28. The overspend reflects rising demand for support that the government's funding formula does not cover for Havering and other councils across England. The council is proceeding with plans to expand specialist provision, including a new SEND unit at R J Mitchell Primary School, to meet the 77 per cent projected increase in pupils with communication and interaction needs by 2028/29. However, the expansion has been approved with the explicit statement that the council will not meet any costs if the school's spending exceeds available funding, leaving responsibility for financial sustainability with the school's governing body.

findings.headline: New mandatory pension pooling regulations came into effect 30 June 2026; Havering signed Investment Management Agreement with London CIV in July 2026
findings.detail: The Pension Schemes Act 2026 and the Local Government Pension Scheme (Pooling, Management and Investment of Funds) Regulations 2026 became effective on 30 June 2026, requiring participation in an FCA-regulated asset pool. Havering complied by executing an Investment Management Agreement with London CIV as a deed in July 2026. This formalises the pool's role in managing the fund "in line with the new LGPS regulations." A Strategic Implementation Plan is due within 90 days.
findings.matters: This represents a significant structural change in fund governance and management; the mandatory pooling model affects how the fund's assets are managed and how the council exercises oversight.
findings.figures: Regulations effective 30 June 2026; IMA executed July 2026; implementation plan due within 90 days
findings.quote: Following the end of the reporting period, the London Borough of Havering entered into and Investment Management Agreement (IMA) with London CIV, which was executed as a deed in July 2026.

findings.headline: Fund holds listed equities at upper tolerance boundary while underweight in alternatives; London CIV to produce rebalancing plan within 90 days
findings.detail: Table 1 shows asset allocation drift across multiple categories. Listed equities stand at 45.9%, at the ceiling of the 35-45% tolerance range. The fund is underweight in alternatives: Private Credit at 6.3% (target 10%), Property/Real Estate at 7.0% (target 12.5%), and Infrastructure at 10.0% (target 12.5%). The fund also holds 4.8% in cash against a zero target. The Investment Management Agreement with London CIV requires rebalancing "including rebalancing any overweight positions" within 90 days.
findings.matters: Asset allocation drift increases portfolio risk; the rebalancing being undertaken by London CIV will affect the fund's risk profile and future returns.
findings.figures: Listed Equity 45.9% (tolerance 35–45%); Private Credit 6.3% (target 10%); Property/Real Estate 7.0% (target 12.5%); Infrastructure 10.0% (target 12.5%); Cash 4.8% (target 0%)
findings.quote: As part of this agreement, London CIV is required to prepare a Strategic Implementation Plan within 90 days of signing, setting out how it will implement the Fund's investment strategy, including rebalancing any overweight positions.

findings.headline: Fund underperformed benchmark in all reporting periods, with 5-year cumulative shortfall of 3.41 percentage points
findings.detail: The Fund delivered a quarterly return of 6.1%, but the paper reports it "underperformed its benchmark in each case." Over five years, the fund returned 4.69% against a benchmark of 8.10%. Underperformance is consistent across all periods: 0.36pp over 3 months, 2.11pp over 12 months, 2.23pp over 3 years, and 3.41pp over 5 years.
findings.matters: Persistent underperformance against benchmark could impact the fund's ability to meet its liabilities, and may eventually require higher employer contribution rates from the council.
findings.figures: Fund 5-year return 4.69% vs Benchmark 8.10%; Fund 3-month return 6.09% vs Benchmark 6.44%
findings.quote: The Fund delivered positive returns across all periods but underperformed its benchmark in each case.

findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy income is under pressure due to the final transfer of clients to Universal Credit and ineligible landlord claims.
findings.detail: Resources is forecasting an overspend of £1m (4% of budget), with Housing Benefit subsidy identified as the main risk. The shortfall is caused by the final transfer of clients from HB to Universal Credit and also by shortfalls where HB has been claimed at Supported/Exempt Accommodation rates but the landlord is not eligible.
findings.matters: HB subsidy income losses indicate the council may face unexpected income shortfalls as government policy shifts towards Universal Credit, reducing the predictability of revenue.
findings.figures: Housing Benefit subsidy shortfall contributing to £1m Resources overspend
findings.quote: The main risk in Resources is the Housing Benefit Subsidy where there is a shortfall leading to a pressure. This is caused by the final transfer of clients from HB to Universal Credit and also by shortfalls where HB has been claimed at Supported/Exempt Accommodation rates but the landlord is not eligible.

findings.headline: The Dedicated Schools Grant shows a cumulative deficit forecast to reach £110m by 2027-28, with a £34.2m overspend this year.
findings.detail: There is a significant continuing overspend in the High Needs Block of the DSG, with a forecasted overspend of £34.2m (100% of the £45.14m block budget). This reflects increasing demand for support that the central government formula does not cover for Havering and other local authorities. Though MHCLG has announced a write-off of up to 90% of deficits due to High Needs pressures, this remains a significant structural pressure dependent on the council submitting an approved SEND Reform Plan.
findings.matters: A £110m accumulated deficit, even with a planned write-off, indicates structural pressure on SEND/High Needs that the council cannot control. The write-off is discretionary and dependent on continued compliance, creating future risk.
findings.figures: £34.2m overspend in High Needs Block (100% of block), cumulative deficit forecast £110m by end 2027-28, planned write-off up to 90%
findings.quote: The cumulative overall DSG deficit forecasted to be carried forward to 2027-28 is expected to be up to £110m.

editorial.headline: Havering's structural deficit forces £37.7m exceptional support; £240m borrowing conversion ahead
editorial.standfirst: July cabinet papers show Havering's structural deficit requiring exceptional support, as £240m internal borrowing converts to external next year.
editorial.body:
Havering's 2025/26 accounts, presented to July's cabinet, reveal structural revenue collapse. The council's net expenditure reached £242.11m against available funding, "necessitating the use [of] Exceptional Financial Support" of £37.7m. This is not a one-off overspend. The council's own papers describe it as "an underlying budget gap" that already requires further exceptional support budgeted for 2026/27.

The deficit masks systemic failure across core services. Within Living Well, Learning Disabilities overspent by £1.95m despite receiving £4.9m additional growth. The council identifies "complexity pressures" as the culprit—spending on high-cost transition cases and client complexity outpacing new resource. Schools have deteriorated sharply: from a £1.86m surplus at the end of 2024/25 to an overall deficit of £0.72m, with 15 schools now in individual deficit totalling £6.3m.

Capital spending has become the council's chronic drag. Outturn was £135.4m against a £163.7m forecast—a £28.4m shortfall the council attributes to "delayed start on site at four schemes approved to start in 2025/26" across Mercury Land Holdings' housing programme. SEND school expansions were hit by "delays in the procurement process and appointment of contractors." Transport for London schemes went undelivered due to "resourcing constraints," leaving grant funding unclaimed. The council requested £125m carry-forward.

Revenue savings delivery collapsed: £1.2m went unachieved, £2.0m delayed to 2026/27.

The 2026/27 outlook will be defined by debt. The council holds £240m of internal borrowing. Papers note "it is highly likely therefore that further new external borrowing will be needed in 2026/27 both to finance that year's capital programme but also to reduce the level of internal borrowing as those funds are needed for other purposes." This conversion will materially increase debt service costs. The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit stands at £69m; a required £6.9m local contribution hinges on DfE SEND Reform Plan approval.
editorial.pull_quote: increasing levels of client complexity, despite adding in £4.9m of growth
editorial.watch_next: The 2026/27 budget setting will formally confirm the external borrowing requirement and DfE SEND Reform Plan approval status.
